# Agent Engineering Standards

An auditable engineering operating model for agent-assisted software work: a machine-readable requirement registry, portable agent role conventions, governance templates, and deterministic scripts — not a prompt library or a RAG platform.

<!-- Generated by scripts/llms-txt-generator.py from registry/tr-registry.yaml, agents/, templates/, and scripts/. Do not edit by hand — regenerate instead. -->

## Start Here

Adoption entry points, shortest path first.

- [AGENTS.starter.md](AGENTS.starter.md) — Seven-rule starter; copy to your project root as AGENTS.md.
- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) — Full tool-neutral conventions; the graduation path from the starter.

## Registry

Machine-readable source: `registry/tr-registry.yaml`.

### Secrets Management

- **TR-SEC-001** — No hardcoded secrets: All secrets must be stored in a vault. Never hardcoded in configuration files, source code, comments, or test fixtures.
- **TR-SEC-008** — Local credential files are permission-restricted and secret-scanned: Files holding secrets on a development or production host (.env files, key files, token caches) must be readable by the owning user only (mode 600). While secrets live in local files rather than a vault (TR-SEC-001's target state), a secret-scanning check must run before commit, not only at public-release time. Counters MITRE ATT&CK T1552.001 (Unsecured Credentials: Credentials in Files).

### Data Privacy

- **TR-SEC-002** — PII encrypted at rest: Personally identifiable information must be encrypted at rest when stored by an application.

### Agents

- **TR-SEC-003** — PII routed to local LLM only: For privacy-focused use cases, local LLMs must be used. Cloud-backed agents must not access private notes, secrets, private repos, or unrestricted home directories.

### Prompt Injection

- **TR-SEC-005** — Externally retrieved content treated as untrusted: Retrieved content must not authorize tool calls or override system-level reasoning. When retrieved content may contain PII, TR-SEC-003 routing takes precedence.
- **TR-SEC-011** — Content provenance tracked and trust derived fail-closed at retrieval: Content ingested into an agentic memory or RAG index must be tagged with its source type at write time. Trust level is derived from source type via a mapping defined in code (not stored as data), so a mapping revision is a code change, not a migration. The mapping is fail-closed: only explicitly named self-authored source types earn the most-trusted tier; any unrecognized or unclassified type falls to the least-trusted tier, and content whose provenance was never recorded is treated as unverified, equivalent to untrusted. Provenance is validated at retrieval time, not only at ingest. Untrusted and unverified content is quarantined data under TR-SEC-005 — spotlighted at the reasoning boundary, never treated as instructions.
- **TR-SEC-012** — Strict LLM output-schema validation — reject, never coerce: Every field returned by a model call must pass both a type check and a range/shape check before use. A field that fails either check must be rejected, never silently coerced to a compatible type. Coercion can fail open: Python's bool("false") evaluates to True because any non-empty string is truthy, so a bare bool() cast on a model-returned string can flip a relevance or safety gate the wrong way. A missing optional field is a defined, valid state; a present field of the wrong type is not, and the two must not share a fallback path. Pairs with TR-GOV-001's single-source-of-truth convention — a strict parser for a given output schema is defined once and used by every caller of that boundary.
- **TR-SEC-015** — Graded outlet confidence never upgrades a TR-SEC-011 trust tier: Alongside the fail-closed trust tier TR-SEC-011 requires, a system may attach an optional, more finely graded confidence about the specific outlet a piece of untrusted content came from (e.g. a curated reference source vs. an unrecognized domain). This tier is informational only: it must never promote content to a more trusted tier, and it must never change how retrieved content is presented at the reasoning boundary — a highly graded outlet's content is still delimited and spotlighted exactly like an ungraded one. The grading source is a small, curated, reviewable allowlist; absence from it is the fail-closed default, never inferred as trustworthy. Downstream weighting or disclosure may read the grade; no trust or spotlighting decision may.

### CI/CD Supply Chain

- **TR-SEC-009** — CI pipelines run least-privilege and fully pinned: Every CI workflow declares an explicit least-privilege permissions block (default contents: read; broader scopes granted per-job with a comment stating why). Third-party CI actions are pinned to a full commit SHA, not a mutable tag, with the human-readable version in a trailing comment. Runtime dependencies past POC tier are pinned to exact versions so the audited dependency set is the set that runs. Counters MITRE ATT&CK T1195 (Supply Chain Compromise) and limits the blast radius of a compromised workflow token.

### Agent Security

- **TR-SEC-010** — Agent tool permission grants are a security boundary (least agency): Permission allowlists for coding agents (e.g. tool-grant or command-allowlist config) are security boundaries, not conveniences: a prompt-injected agent session (TR-SEC-005) can invoke any allowlisted command without human review. Wildcard grants for arbitrary file writes, package installation, unrestricted exec, or unrestricted network access must not be allowlisted; grant the specific command needed instead. This is OWASP's least-agency principle (least privilege extended to what an agent tool can do, how often, and where) applied to agent tooling. Review all agent permission grants at each governance review (TR-GOV-006). Counters MITRE ATT&CK T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter) and T1195.002 executed through trusted developer tooling.
- **TR-SEC-013** — Two-layer isolation for multi-agent tool and data access: When multiple agents share one backing service (a tool surface and the data behind it), isolation must be enforced at two independent layers, not one. Layer one is the tool-registry/authorization scope — distinct credentials per agent, with the server deciding which tools each credential may even invoke; this bounds what is *offered* to a given agent's own reasoning. Layer two is the data-layer scope — per-agent database roles or equivalent, bounding what is *reachable* regardless of what the authorization layer believes it has granted. Neither layer is a substitute for the other: a bug in the tool-registry layer (a stray wildcard registration, a misrouted credential map) can hand an agent a tool it should never have received, and the data-layer role is what still blocks the resulting call; a data layer alone, with no tool-registry scope, would still let a compromised or over-broad tool call reach every table a shared credential can see. Extends TR-SEC-010's least-agency principle from single-agent tool grants to multi-agent tool *and* data boundaries. The most-exposed agent (the one with an external input path) gets the narrowest grant at both layers; the most broadly-privileged agent gets no external egress at all.
- **TR-SEC-014** — Credential-isolated broker operations are scope-bound and single-use: An untrusted or air-gapped agent must not receive credentials for an external system. A host-side broker may expose only named operations; each request must validate the exact resource scope and immutable event identity, bind mutation leases to that identity, revalidate immediately before mutation, and consume each lease exactly once. Broker transport mounts must survive broker restarts without granting the agent write access to the socket directory.

### Testing

- **TR-TEST-001** — TDD required for core logic: Tests are written before or alongside core logic. Scaffolding may come first, but business logic should not be considered complete without tests.
- **TR-TEST-002** — Coverage targets by deployment tier: POC projects may use targeted coverage. Local Production targets at least 70 percent coverage. Cloud Production targets at least 90 percent coverage.
- **TR-TEST-004** — LLM regression benchmark on model switch: When switching or upgrading a runtime LLM, run a standard task set against the old and new models and record cost, latency, correctness, and schema validation deltas. See templates/llm-regression-benchmark.md.
- **TR-TEST-005** — LLM eval files co-located with agent modules: Each agent module that makes LLM calls should have a co-located tests/evals/test_<agent>_eval.py file with golden cases, a score function, and an LLM_EVAL=true guard so evals do not run in the standard unit suite. See templates/llm-eval.md.
- **TR-TEST-006** — Post-write state change verification for agent actions: Agent actions that produce external side effects, such as writing files, updating records, sending messages, or calling tools, should be followed by a deterministic verification step that confirms the observable state changed as expected.
- **TR-TEST-007** — Agent security-property claims verified against ground truth, not self-report: A claim about an agent's own behavior — obtained only by asking the agent in conversation ("do you have tool X," "do you remember Y") — is not verification evidence for a security-relevant property: isolation between agents, a permission boundary, or memory/session scoping. An agent's self-report can produce a false pass when the question is answered by the wrong backend, a stale cache, or the agent's own (possibly incorrect) belief about its state, none of which is the property actually under test. Verify instead against the system's own ground truth — the target API's own list/read endpoint, a database row, a server log line — independent of what the agent under test reports. This is a security-property-specific instance of the general "verify before referencing" discipline (TR-GOV-001's single-source-of-truth cousin, applied to runtime claims rather than static code symbols): the authoritative source for whether an isolation boundary holds is the boundary's own enforcement point, never the agent's narration of it.

### Architecture Decision Records

- **TR-ADR-001** — ADR required for significant design decisions: An ADR must be created for each significant design decision including agent framework choice and trigger classification (TR-AGT-004).
- **TR-GOV-005** — AI system impact assessment: ADRs that change AI behavior toward people require templates/ai-impact-assessment.md.

### Agent Spawning

- **TR-AGT-003** — Agentic node loop contracts: Every agent pipeline node declares input schema, output schema, exit condition, and resource budget before implementation. Nodes exposed as MCP tools additionally declare four tool annotation hints (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) describing blast radius — required only for MCP-exposed nodes. Annotations must be earned, not merely asserted: each hint names a property the implementation actually has, and the test suite must demonstrate it (e.g. idempotentHint requires a real no-op path). Declaring a hint without the property is a protocol violation — callers that retry on a false idempotentHint will amplify damage. A triage or gate node's output schema may additionally include a disposition field drawn from a closed vocabulary (e.g. query / think / report) naming what happens to its output next, derived from the node's own verdict — never set independently of it, so the two cannot disagree. Optional: only nodes whose output routes to more than one next step need to declare it.
- **TR-AGT-002** — Deterministic operations use scripts not agents: Operations that require repeatable results should be implemented in scripts, code, queries, tests, or validators. Agents may call those deterministic tools, but should not replace them.
- **TR-AGT-004** — Agent trigger type classified at design time: Each agent invocation is classified as event-driven, scheduled, or user-initiated. Undocumented triggers are non-compliant unmanaged side effects.
- **TR-AGT-005** — Behavioral mode declaration: A behavioral mode is a named, trigger-activated instruction set that changes how an agent approaches a task, orthogonal to process-intensity gate strictness. Each mode declares a trigger, activated behavior, exit condition, and precedence (safety and process-intensity rules always win on conflict).
- **TR-AGT-006** — Deterministic post-processing over agentic bookkeeping: Agents author content; deterministic code owns structure, indexes, metadata repair, and link integrity. Do not expose bookkeeping that a script can perform reliably as an agent tool the agent may forget to call. Reference shape: a single organize pass (heal → index sync → link check) shared by hook, schedule, CLI, and a read-only health tool.
- **TR-AGT-007** — Self-healing metadata with enrichment marker: When validating persistent records (e.g. note frontmatter), repair missing required fields deterministically and flag inventions with an explicit enrichment marker (e.g. `*_generated: true`) rather than rejecting the record. Remapping a legacy key to its current name is not an invention and must not set the marker. Later agent or human enrichment can target flagged records.
- **TR-AGT-008** — Split agent capabilities by determinism: Classify each capability into one of four tiers before choosing an agent surface: (1) invisible/automatic — no agent surface; (2) agent-invocable tools — genuine judgment calls only; (3) a thin policy skill — instructions for using existing tools well; (4) a CLI that works with no agent present. Deciding test, verbatim: if the agent can forget to run it, it isn't deterministic bookkeeping — it's another judgment call.
- **TR-AGT-009** — Event hooks carry cheap work; schedules carry expensive LLM work: Fire cheap deterministic work from event hooks (post-write heal, index sync). Batch expensive LLM work on a schedule so cost is a function of time, not event volume — N LLM calls in one sitting leave N−1 immediately superseded. Do not attach an LLM call to every ingest or edit event by default.
- **TR-AGT-010** — Tool contracts are frozen, versioned, and generated from live code: A tool surface an agent depends on (an MCP tool set, an internal API a pipeline calls) declares field names and semantics as additive-forever once shipped: existing fields are never removed, renamed, or re-typed, and new fields are always optional. Every structured response — success and error alike — carries a protocol_version that starts at 1 and increments only on a breaking change. The documentation describing the surface (a table of operations, their annotations, their status) is generated from the same live definitions the code registers, not maintained by hand as a separate artifact; a test compares the generated form against what is committed and fails on drift, and a second check compares the declared contract against what the registration code actually sets, so a hand-maintained doc and a hand-maintained declaration cannot silently diverge from each other or from the code. An error response missing protocol_version, or a documented annotation the registration code does not actually set, is a defect, not a documentation gap.
- **TR-AGT-011** — Hybrid deterministic-then-agentic classification tags its own stage: When a classification or triage pipeline runs multiple stages of increasing cost and judgment — a deterministic keyword/rule stage, an optional trained-model stage, an LLM stage — each result carries which stage produced it, from a closed vocabulary declared once and imported everywhere results are constructed. Deterministic stages run first and may short-circuit a later, more expensive stage entirely. A pipeline that has not yet built every stage the vocabulary names must say so rather than fabricate a stage's output to complete the shape — the tag records what actually ran, not what the architecture eventually intends. Reinforces TR-AGT-002 (deterministic checks before agent judgment) and TR-SEC-012 (reject, never coerce, a model's output) at the level of pipeline architecture rather than a single field. A later stage overriding an earlier one on higher confidence is a natural extension of this pattern but is not itself required here — export that as its own practice once a real override path exists to evidence it, rather than asserting it as already covered by this ID.

### Development Conventions

- **TR-GOV-001** — Config/model-string consistency check: scripts/check-config-consistency.py detects retired model strings and drift within an app. Run before merge; CI integration recommended.
- **TR-GOV-002** — Deferred-work tagging convention: Tag deferred work as TECH-DEBT or POC-EXCEPTION. scripts/debt-report.py compiles tags for maturity checklist reconciliation.
- **TR-GOV-003** — Process intensity mode declared per work session: Work sessions may declare a process intensity mode, such as full or poc-fast. Security and agent safety requirements still apply regardless of mode; deferred gates must be recorded as structured debt or POC exceptions.

### App Starter Template

- **TR-GOV-004** — Per-app maturity checklist: Each app maintains docs/maturity-checklist.md mapping governance mechanisms to ISO 42001-inspired control objectives.

### Documentation

- **TR-GOV-006** — Recurring governance review cadence: Governance reviewed at tier graduations and at minimum every 90 days using templates/governance-review.md.
